questions.question: Over one hour, a queue holds $5$ jobs during one episode lasting $10$ minutes and again $5$ jobs during another episode lasting $1$ minute. How do these two episodes enter the time-average number of jobs over this hour, $\frac{1}{60}\int_0^{60}L(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
options: Each episode counts once, since both are single crowded episodes at the same level.
The $10$-minute episode adds ten times as much area as the $1$-minute episode.
Each episode adds its level divided by its duration, so the $1$-minute episode adds ten times as much.
Each episode is weighted by the number of jobs arriving during it.

questions.question: At a post office the number of people present at time $t$ is $L(t)$. Which of the following performance measures is a time average of the state $L$?
options: The fraction of customers who find three or more people present when they arrive.
The mean waiting time in the queue over the first $1000$ customers to arrive.
The long-run fraction of the opening hours with three or more people present.
The fraction of customers whose time in the post office exceeds $30$ minutes.

questions.question: For the number of jobs $L(s)$ in a queueing system, which expression is the long-run fraction of time during which at least $n$ jobs are present?
options: $\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t\mathbf{1}\{L(s)>n\}\,\mathrm{d}s$
$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\,\mathbf{1}\{L(t)\ge n\}$
$\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N\mathbf{1}\{L(A_k-)\ge n\}$
$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{t}\int_0^t\mathbf{1}\{L(s)\ge n\}\,\mathrm{d}s$

questions.question: A queueing system has time-average state probabilities $p(n)=\lim_{t\to\infty}Y(n,t)/t$, where $Y(n,t)$ is the time spent with $n$ jobs during $[0,t]$. Which expression gives the time-average number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]$ (assuming limit and sum may be interchanged)?
options: $\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_n n\,p(n)$, since $L(s)=\sum_n n\,\mathbf{1}\{L(s)=n\}$
$\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_n p(n)$, adding the fractions of time of all states
$\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_n n\,Y(n,t)$ for a large $t$, the total job-time accumulated
$\mathbb{E}[L]=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{n=0}^m n$ over the levels $0,\dots,m$ visited

questions.question: In a single-server queueing system with time-average state probabilities $p(n)$, what does $1-p(0)$ measure?
options: The long-run fraction of arriving jobs that must wait before service starts.
The long-run fraction of time with at least one job waiting in the queue.
The long-run fraction of time that the server is busy serving a job.
The long-run fraction of jobs that are served without any interruption.

questions.question: A single-server system has number-in-system path $L(t)=0$ on $[0,2)$, $1$ on $[2,6)$, $3$ on $[6,7)$, $1$ on $[7,9)$ and $0$ on $[9,10]$ (minutes). What is the time average $\frac{1}{10}\int_0^{10}L(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
options: $1.0$ jobs
$9$ jobs
$9/7\approx1.29$ jobs
$0.9$ jobs

questions.question: A two-server system is observed during $[0,40]$ minutes. The times spent with $0$, $1$, $2$ and $3$ jobs present are $Y(0,40)=10$, $Y(1,40)=18$, $Y(2,40)=8$ and $Y(3,40)=4$ minutes. With $L_s(t)=\min\{L(t),2\}$ the number of jobs in service, what is the time average $\frac{1}{40}\int_0^{40}L_s(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$?
A queueing system has time-average state probabilities $p(0)=0.5$, $p(1)=0.25$, $p(2)=0.15$, $p(3)=0.1$ and $p(n)=0$ for $n\ge4$. What is the time-average number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]$?

Over $20$ days the inventory level $I(t)$ of an item (on-hand stock minus backlog) is $3$ for $8$ days, $1$ for $6$ days, $0$ for $2$ days and $-2$ for $4$ days. What is the time-average inventory level $\frac{1}{20}\int_0^{20}I(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$?

A simulation of a queue starts empty and serves $5$ jobs with sojourn times $J=(3,2,4,1,2)$ minutes; the system is empty again at the last departure $D_5=10$ minutes. What is the estimate $\bar L$ of the time-average number of jobs over $[0,10]$?

The number of jobs $L(t)$ in a queue stays between $0$ and $5$ at all times. A student proposes to estimate the time-average number of jobs by $L(t)/t$ for a large $t$. What does $L(t)/t$ do as $t\to\infty$?
options: It converges to $\mathbb{E}[L]$, since both divide a quantity by the elapsed time $t$.
It converges to the arrival rate $\lambda$, the long-run number of arrivals per unit time.
It converges to $1-p(0)$, since it measures the busy time per unit of elapsed time.
It tends to $0$ for this bounded path, so it carries no information about $\mathbb{E}[L]$.

questions.question: A queue starts empty at time $0$ and is empty again just after the $n$-th departure $D_n$. Job $k$ arrives at $A_k$ and leaves at $D_k$, with sojourn time $J_k=D_k-A_k$. Why does $\int_0^{D_n}L(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=\sum_{k=1}^nJ_k$ hold?
options: Job $k$ adds $1$ to $L(s)$ exactly for $s\in[A_k,D_k)$, so the area splits into $n$ strips of lengths $J_k$.
The server works during $[0,D_n]$ exactly the total service time, and each $J_k$ is a service time.
Jobs leave in arrival order under first-come-first-served, which is needed to match departures to arrivals.
The path $L(s)$ is constant between departures, so the area is a sum of $n$ rectangles ending at the $D_k$.

questions.question: In a single-server system, jobs arrive exactly every $10$ minutes and each needs $10-\epsilon$ minutes of service, with $0<\epsilon<10$. Which statement about the time-average number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]$ and what arriving jobs see is correct?
options: Both averages agree, since regularly spaced arrivals sample the path uniformly.
$\mathbb{E}[L]=1-\epsilon/10$ tends to $1$ as $\epsilon\to0$, while every arrival still finds the system empty.
$\mathbb{E}[L]=1-\epsilon/10$, and a fraction $\epsilon/10$ of the arrivals find the system empty.
$\mathbb{E}[L]=0$, because each job leaves before the next one arrives.

questions.question: A single-server system is empty at times $0$ and $12$ minutes. During $[0,12]$ exactly four jobs arrive and depart, with service times $2$, $3$, $1.5$ and $2.5$ minutes; their sojourn times add up to $12$ minutes. What fraction of the window $[0,12]$ is the server busy?

Over $[0,12]$ minutes the number of jobs is $L=1$ on $[0,3)$, $2$ on $[3,6)$, $3$ on $[6,7)$, $1$ on $[7,9)$ and $0$ on $[9,12]$. What is the fraction of time $\frac{1}{12}\int_0^{12}\mathbf{1}\{L(s)\le1\}\,\mathrm{d}s$?

A single-server queue has time-average state probabilities $p(0)=0.4$, $p(1)=0.3$, $p(2)=0.2$, $p(3)=0.1$. With $Q(t)=\max\{L(t)-1,0\}$ the number waiting in queue, what is the time-average number in queue $\mathbb{E}[Q]$?

A single server without blocking receives jobs at rate $\lambda=0.5$ per minute, and each job needs $\mathbb{E}[S]=3$ minutes, so $\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]=1.5$. Which statement about the long-run fraction of time $1-p(0)$ that the server is busy is correct?
options: It equals $1.5$, because $1-p(0)=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ holds for every single-server queue.
It is at most $1$; $1-p(0)=\lambda\mathbb{E}[S]$ needs rate stability, which fails since $\delta\le1/3<\lambda$.
It equals $1/1.5\approx0.67$, the reciprocal of the load once the queue is overloaded.
It equals $0.5$, since each arrival per minute keeps the server busy for one unit of time.

questions.question: A queueing system has time-average state probabilities $p(n)$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$. How does the time-average number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]=\sum_n n\,p(n)$ compare with the fraction of time $1-p(0)$ that the system is non-empty?
options: $\mathbb{E}[L]=1-p(0)$ always, since a non-empty single server holds one job in service.
$\mathbb{E}[L]\le1-p(0)$, since jobs are present only during the non-empty fraction of time.
Either order is possible, depending on how long the service times are.
$\mathbb{E}[L]\ge1-p(0)$, with equality exactly when two or more jobs are present a fraction $0$ of the time.

questions.question: A single first-come-first-served server starts empty; jobs arrive at $A=(0,1,3)$ minutes with service times $S=(2,2,3)$, so they leave at $D=(2,4,7)$. What is the time average $\frac{1}{5}\int_0^5L(s)\,\mathrm{d}s$ over the window $[0,5]$?

Jobs arrive at a single server every $10$ minutes starting at time $0$; their service times alternate $12,6,12,6,\dots$ minutes, served first-come-first-served. What is the time-average number of jobs $\mathbb{E}[L]$ in the system?
